subject: SOCIAL STUDIES
title: Aspects of Traditional Culture in the County
overview: Culture is the way of life of a group of people. In this sub-strand you will identify six aspects of traditional culture: dressing, food, housing, artefacts, sports and games, and festivals and ceremonies. You will find out how the communities in your county practised them, show them through pictures, songs and objects, and explain why culture is important.

lessons.title: What is traditional culture? Dressing, food and housing
objectives: Explain the meaning of culture and traditional culture.
Describe traditional dressing, food and housing of communities in the county.
lessons.intro: Think about the food your grandparents ate when they were children, the clothes they wore on special days and the houses they lived in. These things tell us a lot about the way of life of your community long ago.
lessons.notes:
Culture is the way of life of a group of people. It includes what they eat, what they wear, the houses they build, the tools they make, the games they play and the ceremonies they hold. Traditional culture is the way of life that a community has practised for a long time and passed on from grandparents to parents to children.

Kenya has many communities, and each county is home to one or more of them. Each community has its own culture, so the aspects of culture you find in your county may be different from those in another county.

### Dressing
Long ago, people made clothes from materials found around them, such as animal skins, bark of trees and leaves. Many communities decorated themselves with beads, feathers, shells and metal bangles. Some decorations showed a person's age or position in the community. At the coast, people wear the kanga and kikoi, which are pieces of printed cloth.

### Food
Traditional foods came from the crops people grew, the animals they kept, the fish they caught and the wild fruits and vegetables they gathered. Examples in Kenya include ugali, porridge made from millet or sorghum, githeri (maize and beans cooked together), fermented milk, fish, meat and traditional vegetables such as managu (African nightshade), terere (amaranth) and kunde (cowpea leaves).

### Housing
Traditional houses were built with materials found nearby: poles, mud, grass, reeds, papyrus, stones or palm leaves. Many houses were round with a grass-thatched roof. Communities that moved from place to place with their animals built houses that were easy to put up and take down.

### Finding out about your county
Ask your parents, grandparents and other elders which community or communities live in your county and how they dressed, what they ate and how they built their houses. Write down what they tell you.

examples.problem: Name three materials that were used to build traditional houses.
steps: Think of what was found near homes long ago.
examples.answer: Any three, for example poles, mud, grass, reeds, stones or palm leaves.

activity.title: Brainstorm aspects of culture
steps: In groups, brainstorm the traditional foods, dressing and houses of the communities in your county.
Write your ideas under three headings: Dressing, Food and Housing.
Each group describes one aspect to the class.
At home, ask an elder to tell you one more traditional food or type of dressing and add it to your list.

practice.question: What is culture?
practice.answer: Culture is the way of life of a group of people.

practice.question: Name two traditional foods eaten in Kenya.
practice.answer: Any two, for example ugali, millet porridge, githeri, fermented milk, fish or traditional vegetables such as managu.

practice.question: Why did people long ago build houses using grass, mud and poles?
practice.answer: Because these materials were found near their homes.

summary: Culture is the way of life of a group of people.
Traditional dressing, food and housing came from materials found around the community.
Elders are a good source of information about the culture of your county.

lessons.title: Artefacts, sports and games, festivals and ceremonies
objectives: Identify traditional artefacts and their uses.
Name traditional sports, games, festivals and ceremonies.
lessons.intro: Have you seen a clay pot, a woven basket or a wooden stool in your grandparents' home? These objects were made by hand long ago, and many families still use them today.
lessons.notes:
### Artefacts
Artefacts are objects made by people, especially long ago. They show the skills and way of life of a community. Traditional artefacts include:

- Clay pots for cooking and storing water
- Baskets and mats woven from reeds, sisal or grass
- Gourds or calabashes for storing milk and water
- Wooden stools, spoons and bowls
- Musical instruments such as drums, horns and stringed instruments
- Tools and weapons such as hoes, spears, shields, bows and arrows

### Sports and games
Traditional sports and games were played for fun, for exercise and to teach skills such as counting, running and hunting. Examples include wrestling, running races, spear throwing, bull fighting in some communities, and board games such as bao, which is played with seeds on a board with holes. Children played skipping games, hide and seek and singing games.

### Festivals and ceremonies
Ceremonies are special events held to mark important stages in life. Common traditional ceremonies include:

- Naming ceremonies, when a baby is given a name
- Initiation ceremonies, when young people move from childhood to adulthood
- Wedding ceremonies
- Funeral ceremonies
- Harvest festivals, to celebrate and give thanks for a good harvest

During ceremonies people sang traditional songs, danced, ate special foods and wore special dress. Songs carried messages. There were songs for weddings, for naming, for initiation and for victory.

Some aspects of culture are still practised today, while others have changed or stopped. For example, many people still eat traditional foods and sing traditional songs, but few people wear animal skins as everyday clothing.

keyWords.meaning: an object made by people, especially long ago
a special event held to mark an important occasion
a time of celebration for a community

examples.problem: Give one use of a traditional clay pot.
steps: Think of what pots hold.

examples.problem: Which ceremony is held when a baby is given a name?
steps: Match the event to its ceremony.

activity.title: Describe the aspects of culture
materials: Pictures of artefacts, games and ceremonies
Real artefacts from home, if available
steps: In groups, look at the pictures and any artefacts brought to class.
Describe each artefact: what it is made of and what it was used for.
Play one traditional game that a group member knows and explain its rules.
Name one ceremony practised in your community and describe what happens during it.

practice.question: What is an artefact?
practice.answer: An object made by people, especially long ago, such as a pot, basket or stool.

practice.question: Name two traditional ceremonies.
practice.answer: Any two, for example naming, initiation, wedding, funeral or harvest ceremonies.

practice.question: Give one reason why traditional games were played.
practice.answer: For fun, for exercise, or to teach skills such as counting and running.

summary: Artefacts include pots, baskets, gourds, stools, tools and musical instruments.
Traditional games entertained people and taught skills.
Ceremonies marked important stages in life, such as naming, initiation and marriage.

lessons.title: Showcasing and appreciating traditional culture
objectives: Collect and record aspects of traditional culture practised in the community.
Explain why traditional culture is important.
lessons.intro: A culture day at school is a chance to show traditional dress, songs, dances and foods. Each learner can bring something from home that tells the story of their community.
lessons.notes:
### Illustrating culture
To illustrate means to show something so that others can see and understand it. You can illustrate aspects of traditional culture by:

- Drawing or painting pictures of traditional houses, dress and artefacts
- Collecting photographs from home, with permission
- Bringing artefacts such as baskets, gourds or stools to class
- Learning and performing traditional songs and dances
- Preparing a traditional food with the help of an adult
- Making models of traditional houses using clay, sticks and grass

When you collect items, record what each item is, what it is made of, what it was used for and who told you about it. Handle borrowed items with care and return them.

### Why culture is important
Traditional culture is important because:

- It gives people an identity. It tells us who we are and where we come from.
- It teaches good values such as respect for elders, hard work and sharing.
- It unites members of a community when they meet for ceremonies and festivals.
- Traditional foods are often healthy and made from local crops.
- It keeps useful skills alive, such as weaving, pottery and carving.
- It entertains people through songs, dances and games.
- It attracts tourists, who come to see traditional dances, crafts and ways of life.
- Learning about the culture of others helps us respect them and live in peace.

Every community's culture is special. We should respect the cultures of other people, just as we want them to respect ours. At the same time, practices that harm people, such as female genital mutilation and early marriage, should not be continued.

keyWords.meaning: to show something using pictures, objects or performances
who a person or community is
a person who travels to a place for pleasure and to learn

examples.problem: Give two ways of showcasing traditional culture in class.
steps: Think of things you can show, perform or make.
examples.answer: Any two, for example drawing traditional houses, displaying artefacts, performing traditional songs and dances, or making models.

activity.title: Culture corner showcase
materials: Artefacts, pictures or photographs from home
Clay, sticks and grass for models
steps: Collect and record one aspect of traditional culture practised in your community: a picture, song, artefact, piece of dress, food, painting or tool.
Write a label for it: its name, what it is made of and what it is used for.
Set up a culture corner in class with your group's items.
Take turns to showcase your items to other groups, sing a traditional song or explain a traditional game.
As a class, list reasons why traditional culture is important.

practice.question: Give three reasons why traditional culture is important.
practice.answer: Any three, for example it gives identity, teaches good values, unites people, keeps skills alive, entertains and attracts tourists.

practice.question: How can you record an artefact you have collected?
practice.answer: Write its name, what it is made of, what it is used for and who told you about it.

practice.question: Why should we respect the culture of other communities?
practice.answer: Because every culture is special, and respecting others helps us live in peace.

summary: We can illustrate culture through drawings, artefacts, songs, dances, foods and models.
Culture gives identity, teaches values, unites people and attracts tourists.
Respect other cultures, but harmful practices should be stopped.

lessons.title: Songs, dances and culture we still practise
objectives: Illustrate traditional culture through songs and dances from the community.
Explain which aspects of culture are still practised and why they should be appreciated.
lessons.intro: A wedding, a naming day or a harvest celebration is often full of song. The words, the drums and the dance steps are another way a community shows its culture.
lessons.notes:
Culture is not only what people eat or wear. It is also heard and seen when people sing and dance. Traditional songs and dances carry messages. They entertain people, and they teach the young about the life of the community.

### Songs for different occasions
Communities sang different songs for different events:

- Naming songs, sung when a baby is given a name
- Wedding songs, sung when two people marry
- Initiation songs, sung when young people are prepared for adulthood
- Victory songs, sung after a success such as a good harvest or a contest
- Work songs, sung while people farmed, fished or built, so that the work felt lighter

The words of a song may praise a person, give advice, tell a story or thank God for a harvest. Dances use steps, clapping and instruments such as drums, horns and shakers. Costumes and body decoration used in the dance are part of traditional dressing.

### Culture then and now
Some aspects of culture are still practised today. Many families still eat traditional foods, wear traditional dress on special days, and sing traditional songs. Other aspects have changed. Few people now build only grass houses or wear animal skins every day, because new materials and new ways of living have come.

Ask an elder which aspects of your community's culture are still practised and which have stopped. Record the answer. A good record names the aspect, describes it, and says who taught you.

### Appreciating culture
We appreciate culture when we learn it, perform it with respect and teach it to others. Appreciating culture does not mean copying every old practice. Practices that harm people, such as female genital mutilation and early marriage, should stop. Songs, foods, crafts, games and peaceful ceremonies should be kept, because they give us identity, bring people together and can attract visitors who want to learn.

keyWords.meaning: a song passed down in a community and sung at special occasions
movement, often with music, used to celebrate or to pass a message
to value something and show that it matters

examples.problem: A class learns a wedding song from an elder and performs it on culture day. Which aspect of culture are they illustrating?
steps: The song belongs to a ceremony and is performed for others to see and hear.
examples.answer: Festivals and ceremonies, shown through traditional music and dance.

examples.problem: Name one aspect of culture that many families still practise, and one harmful practice that should stop.
steps: Think of food, dress or songs that continue.
Think of practices that injure children.
examples.answer: Still practised: traditional foods, dress on special days, or traditional songs. Should stop: female genital mutilation or early marriage.

activity.title: Showcase a traditional song or dance
materials: A drum, shaker or clapping if available
steps: Ask a parent, guardian or grandparent to teach you one traditional song or dance from your community. Note the occasion it is used for.
In groups, practise the song or dance. Write the message the song carries.
Showcase it to the class. Other learners listen respectfully, even if the song is from a community different from theirs.
Record the performance on paper: the name of the song, the occasion, the instruments and who taught you.
Discuss which aspects of culture your families still practise and why those aspects are important.

practice.question: Give two occasions when traditional songs are sung.
practice.answer: Any two, for example naming, wedding, initiation, victory or work.

practice.question: What two things can a traditional song do for a community?
practice.answer: It can carry a message and it can entertain. It can also teach the young.

practice.question: Why should we keep traditional songs but stop harmful practices?
practice.answer: Songs give identity, teach and bring people together. Harmful practices such as female genital mutilation injure people and are against the law.

summary: Songs and dances illustrate culture and carry messages for naming, weddings, initiation and work.
Some aspects of culture continue today, while others have changed.
Appreciate useful culture, and do not continue practices that harm people.

quiz.question: What is culture?
options: The way of life of a group of people
quiz.explanation: Culture is the way of life of a group of people.

quiz.question: Which of these is an aspect of traditional culture?
quiz.explanation: Dressing is one of the six aspects of culture in this sub-strand.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a traditional artefact?
quiz.explanation: A calabash or gourd is a traditional container made by hand.

quiz.question: What ceremony marks the move from childhood to adulthood?
quiz.explanation: Initiation ceremonies mark the change from childhood to adulthood.

quiz.question: Name the six aspects of traditional culture studied in this sub-strand.
quiz.answer: Dressing, food, housing, artefacts, sports and games, and festivals and ceremonies.
quiz.explanation: These are the six aspects listed in the curriculum.

quiz.question: Traditional houses were built using materials such as:
quiz.explanation: People used materials found near their homes, such as mud, poles and grass.

quiz.question: Which is a good way to illustrate traditional housing in class?
options: Making a model with clay, sticks and grass
quiz.explanation: A model shows what a traditional house looked like.

quiz.question: When you borrow an artefact from home for a culture corner, what should you do?
quiz.answer: Handle it with care, label it and return it.
quiz.explanation: Artefacts are valuable to families and should be kept safe.

quiz.question: Which is an importance of traditional culture?
quiz.explanation: Culture tells us who we are and where we come from.

quiz.question: How does traditional culture help the country earn money?
quiz.answer: It attracts tourists who come to see traditional dances, crafts and ways of life.
quiz.explanation: Tourists pay for visits, crafts and services.

quiz.question: Which traditional practice should NOT be continued?
quiz.explanation: Female genital mutilation harms girls and is against the law in Kenya.

quiz.question: A naming song is an example of culture shown through:
quiz.explanation: Naming songs are sung at naming ceremonies and carry a message from the community.
